articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang scandal makes Congress a bigger risk to U.S.-China relations
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang scandal makes Congress a bigger risk to U.S.-China relations
articles.content_orig:
Trade tensions between the U.S. and China may resurface in 2027 as a Democrat-controlled Congress tightens chip export controls, economists told CNBC, ahead of a closely watched meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping.
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a woman suspected by the U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy has already led to efforts seeking stricter curbs on tech exports.
In the U.S.' first policy response to the Huang scandal, the Commerce Department on Monday took steps to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries.
Beijing has yet not issued a response to the U.S. move that comes ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting on Thursday.
"Jensen-Gate" may accentuate the tensions and reinforce bilateral posturing but does not constitute a "tectonic shift," said Vishnu Varathan, head of economics and strategy at Mizuho Bank.
The world's top two economies have seen improvement in relations since Trump and Xi reached a trade truce last year, meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The number of times the two leaders have met, and plan to meet, this year does signal movement in a positive direction, said Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management.
Now as they prepare to engage at APEC again, does "Jensen-Gate" risk hurting that relationship materially?
"Our base case is that it won't derail the leader-level relationship in the near term," said Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management, in an emailed response to questions. "The bigger risk is that it gives Congress a reason to tighten tech controls over the next 6–12 months."
Both Beijing and Washington need a win but that's far from assured.
At stake is China's tech manufacturing export boom supporting an otherwise uneven domestic economy that remains mired in deflation, sluggish consumer confidence and a property market that's yet to stage a durable recovery.
President Trump and top trade policy officials are looking to extend a trade truce beyond Jan. 10, amid cost-of-living challenges caused by the Iran war that cost the governing Republican Party the Midterms and ceded control of Congress to the Democrats.
The Huang scandal and the Midterm losses could, however, complicate the temporary U.S.-China trade and tariffs deal, with lawmakers asking for tougher tech curbs.
"Post-Midterms dynamics give Congress (especially Democrats) more leverage to press for harder export controls or to criticize any perceived softness," said Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis. "Markets have largely treated the truce as durable stability; the risk of renewed escalation if compliance disputes, political pressure, or the Huang investigations intensify is real."
The rise of tough-on-China policy hawks on Capitol Hill is not lost on Beijing.
An article in state media China Daily on Monday noted the political firestorm surrounding Nvidia soon after the Midterms is "considerably more" than a company or the conduct of its former chief executive. "Its timing, the congressional reaction and the legislative ambitions now gathering momentum in Washington point to a larger objective: building political support for tougher high-tech restrictions against China."
Highline's Emons defined a 'smoking gun' scenario as "a confirmed [China] Ministry of State Security link plus evidence that chips were diverted."
Should that materialize, "that would most likely push Congress toward veto-style review of chip sales. Beijing's answer would come through rare earths and its own export controls. I'd put that at roughly 20–25% over six months. That's low, but it isn't priced," Emons said.
Chris Miller, associate professor of international history at The Fletcher School, Tufts University, said "if they find malpractice, Congress is likely to pass legislation that Beijing does not like."
Leading Trump administration officials together with Republicans and Democrats in Congress are "laser focused on this question of tech export controls," Miller told " Squawk Box Asia " on Monday, adding that chips and chip-making equipment could face "intensified restrictions over the coming months."
What many trade policy watchers find ironic is that China has held off from approving purchases of Nvidia H200 chips to build domestic chip self-reliance even after Washington cleared their exports. That illustrates how "Beijing needs Nvidia less than Nvidia needs China," Highline's Emons said.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures are mixed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures are mixed after Nvidia pressures tech to start the week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures were mixed early Tuesday, following a losing session as Nvidia weighed on the tech sector.
S&P 500 futures were flat, Dow Jones Industrial Average futures fell 0.32%, while Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.21%.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 1.42% and South Korea's Kospi dropped 2.05%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed 1.76% lower. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 0.76%, while mainland China's CSI 300 was flat.
In regular U.S. trading Monday, Nvidia shares pulled back 4.1%, as traders dumped the chipmaker ahead of its fiscal third-quarter report, due Tuesday after the bell. Other stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell as well, including AMD, Micron Technology and Sandisk.
"The tape feels increasingly fragile as Nvidia's AI premium continues to unwind and investors reassess the durability of the ecosystem built around its dominance," said Ben Emons, founder of FedWatch Advisors, in a note. "This backdrop has fueled the 'dispersion trade,' gradually eroding the extreme concentration that has defined the S&P 500 and Nasdaq."
Nvidia has been tumbling since last week. Jensen Huang resigned from the CEO post Thursday after reports emerged that he had multiple affairs , including one with an alleged Chinese spy . Further, the chipmaker's board of directors is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The stock has dropped almost 24% this month, putting it on pace for its biggest monthly decline since April 2022 — when it plunged 32%.
The 30-stock Dow on Monday slid more than 700 points, or 1.4%, while the S&P 500 lost 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.5%, its biggest one-day decline since Nov. 5.
On Tuesday, investors will pore through a slew of economic data, including October retail sales and import prices. On the earnings front, Disney and Home Depot are set to report before the opening bell.
Oil prices fell Tuesday as expectations of a global supply surplus outweighed concerns over continued attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping in the Middle East.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude fell 0.71% to $92.44 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures declined 0.69% to $85.72 a barrel.
The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil market was expected to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, as Middle East exports recover faster than demand.
Meanwhile, oil cartel OPEC met virtually on Monday to review members' maximum sustainable production capacity, a measure used to help determine future output quotas. The broader OPEC+ alliance, which includes Russia, is scheduled to meet Nov. 29 to discuss production policy for 2027.
Shares of Chinese internet search engine Baidu fell 6.25% in Hong Kong on Tuesday after the company reported a 1% year-over-year decline in third-quarter revenue to 30.8 billion yuan ($4.6 billion).
Baidu's online marketing services revenue dropped 22% from a year earlier to 11.9 billion yuan, while its revenue from its AI cloud infrastructure business surged 94%.
The company's U.S.-listed shares closed 5.37% lower on Monday.
Major Asian technology stocks fell on Tuesday after Nvidia shares extended losses in U.S. after hours trading, as uncertainty persisted over the chipmaker's leadership following Jensen Huang's departure. Nvidia is searching for a new CEO, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered more than 180,000 signatures.
Japan's SoftBank Group dropped 4.68% in early trading.
In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics fell 1.52% and 2.34%, respectively, dragging down the benchmark Kospi index.
Asia-Pacific markets opened lower on Tuesday.
Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 0.76%, while the Topix declined 1.06%. South Korea's Kospi dropped 1.57%, and the small-cap Kosdaq lost 0.62%.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.37%.
Asia-Pacific markets were set to fall Tuesday, tracking sharp declines in U.S. equity benchmarks overnight.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 59,075 while in Osaka they were last at 59,200, compared with the index's previous close of 59,662.02.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,669 compared with the index's last close of 23,753.84.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 1.30% in early trade.
Wall Street's big bets came into view on Monday, as major investors released their latest 13F filings, which show where they put their money to work by the end of the third quarter.
Among the notable moves during the period were D1 Capital Partners increasing its positions in Lattice Semiconductor and chip materials supplier Qnity Electronics .
Check out CNBC Pro's roundup below for more.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures added 34 points, or 0.1%. S&P 500 futures gained 0.1%, and Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.2%.

articles.title_orig: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.title_zh: The Death of ‘Keep 1.5 Alive’
articles.content_orig:
ANTALYA, Turkey — “Anything is possible if you believe,” croons Turkish pop megastar Tarkan in his theme song for this year’s global COP31 climate conference.
Attendees appear to have taken his words to heart.
The Antalya summit marks the first climate talks since the United Nations told the world global warming would soon exceed 1.5C, effectively burying the totemic Paris Agreement target that has steered COP negotiations for more than a decade.
Yet leaders here are straining to keep the goal on life support.
“We are on course to overshoot the 1.5 degree target, and every fraction of a degree matters. So we must double down,” said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her speech to fellow leaders on Wednesday.
“Let’s show that the fight for 1.5C is not over,” Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands told leaders.
Even before the talks began, Danish Climate Minister Samira Nawa told POLITICO her country’s priority at COP31 was “to push for keeping the 1.5C target in the heart of global climate ambitions.”
Other leaders and ministers, reviving slogans from COPs past, have exhorted their colleagues to “keep 1.5 alive” or ensure the target remains “within reach.”
But scientists say that dream is over.
The U.N. last month said that, even if countries dramatically slash planet-warming emissions starting right now, the best outcome would be a rise in global temperatures of 1.8 degrees. If they also deploy vast amounts of carbon removal tech to clean up the atmosphere, there’s a chance of getting back to 1.5 degrees after surpassing it — in theory.
In reality, though, greenhouse gas emissions are still rising and the carbon-hoovering technologies needed to achieve that reversal are unproven at scale.
The collective ambition of national climate plans, already insufficient before the U.N.’s announcement, is even weaker than projected last year. Countries that have been among the strongest proponents of meeting the 1.5-degree target are watering down efforts to achieve it.
But at the same time, many countries (and climate scientists) fear that publicly dumping the rhetoric around 1.5C will open the door to weakening global ambitions even further. Highlighting other possible targets, such as the 1.8C mentioned by the U.N., would be a “slippery slope,” warned one European climate negotiator.
“I do not support the political messaging of keeping 1.5C alive — but on the other hand, I don't want to lose it,” said Johan Rockström, a leading climate scientist and director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.
“Politicians, when they say that, may naively think that we somehow still are on this linear, incremental journey that can simply take us to safety, which is not the case,” he added. “On the other hand, if we scientifically criticize it, the risk is that they do indeed say: ‘OK, let's just drop it and aim for 2 degrees instead,' which would be a big mistake.”
For island nations already losing land and livelihoods to rising oceans, the 1.5 degree target is not merely symbolic. It represents their very survival.
“Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over,” said Heine, the Marshall Islands president. “Overshoot means waves eating away our shores, flooding that destroys towns, schools, hospitals. It destroys our land and ocean.”
The temperature target was not chosen arbitrarily. It represents the level of warming scientists say the planet can endure before the heat trapped in the atmosphere unleashes exponentially greater dangers.
In the Paris accord, countries vowed to limit warming to below 2 degrees and “ideally” 1.5 degrees. The second target has become so dominant that the International Court of Justice last year declared it the primary goal.
A group of developed and highly vulnerable nations, known as the High Ambition Coalition, have called for a credible response to the overshoot as one key COP31 outcome.
“There is no way we can lose that anchor, out of our moral responsibility toward the people who have contributed the least and are the most impacted,” said Christiana Figueres, who headed the U.N. climate body when the Paris Agreement was adopted.
But promises have not aligned with reality.
“Leaders, and in particular those from developed countries, cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders in his opening speech on Wednesday.
Yet immediately after his speech, leaders did just that.
Australia, COP31 co-hosts with Turkey, is expanding investments in coal and natural gas, even as its Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen urges leaders in Antalya to act with “urgency, solidarity and resolve.”
“With every minute that we fail to achieve the targets set out in the Paris Agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Two days earlier, he had celebrated the discovery of two new oil fields.
“The science is clear. Breaching 1.5 isn’t where we down tools and give up,” Katie White, the U.K.’s climate minister, said in response to the U.N. findings. White promised COP31 was the place to double down on action — but a day later, her own department approved a major natural gas project in the North Sea.
Meanwhile the United States, the largest polluter in world history , has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and is no longer part of COP talks. Donald Trump’s abandonment of efforts to address global warming has left a large gap in the world’s collective efforts to cut emissions.
Tina Stege, the Marshall Islands’ climate envoy, acknowledged the difficulty of the challenge. But she was unbending.
“That's not a reason to not do everything that we absolutely can,” she told reporters. “Every country that showed up at this talk to do the work needs to do that work and more.”
Doing more means ramping up clean electrification and alternative fuels, say experts.
It also means dramatically curbing short-term climate pollutants, such as methane. That’s emerging as a possible response to the overshoot declaration in the final agreement from this year’s negotiations, according to the European diplomat cited above.
“If we cut methane by nearly half by 2030, we could avoid almost 0.3 degrees of warming by the 2040s and save 250,000 lives every year,” said Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, on Wednesday. “This buys us the time to get back to the 1.5 degrees.”
The politics are tricky. Even as technological advances have allowed for better detection of the potent pollutant, the U.S. and Europe have weakened regulations aimed at curbing methane emissions.
Mottley was adamant nonetheless that flagging global ambitions were no reason to give up.
“I call for a global movement: 1.5 billion voices for 1.5 degrees,” she said. “We need to do this before we meet at COP32 next year. … Make 1.5 impossible to ignore on the planet Earth.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Will Miss Most of the ASEAN Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump Will Miss Most of the ASEAN Summit
articles.content_orig:
For the second year in a row, President Trump is attending the annual gathering of Southeast Asian leaders, a show of alliance to a region that the United States sees as a strategic and maritime counterweight to China.
But Mr. Trump will reach the gathering, held this year in Manila, only on Tuesday, just as the summit wraps up, and he is not expected to make any significant policies or diplomacy moves.
Mixed signals like this — to say nothing of Mr. Trump’s punishing tariffs — are adding to a widespread belief within ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, that the United States is not a reliable partner. That leaves the bloc balancing between Washington and Beijing, with which many of its members have deep trade partnerships.
“They’ve learned that the United States is not reliable, so a lot of the hedging has been away from the United States,” said Ted Osius, a former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam.
The Philippines, America’s oldest security ally in Asia, provides a window into this balancing act.
After taking office three years ago, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reversed his predecessor’s tilt toward China and pivoted back toward the United States. That stance contributed to many tense encounters between Filipino and Chinese vessels in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing territorial claims.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress to make her debut at first earnings
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress to make her debut at first earnings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Jensen Huang built Nvidia (NVDA) into the company that powers the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Over 33 years, Huang transformed a graphics-chip maker into a $4 trillion technology powerhouse. Replacing someone with that kind of track record would be difficult under the best circumstances. Doing so amid scandal, plunging share prices, and growing concerns about the AI boom makes the challenge considerably greater.
Yet Nvidia's decision to name Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress the interim CEO could be precisely what the company needs.
Why It's Time to Load Up on CoreWeave Stock
Dear AST SpaceMobile Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 17
How to Play Alibaba Stock Ahead of Its T-Head Spinoff and IPO
Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.
Kress doesn't have Huang's celebrity status or reputation as a tech visionary. What she brings instead is something Nvidia investors might appreciate even more right now: financial discipline and the willingness to challenge the company's biggest bets.
And that could make her a better choice than many investors realize.
Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 after holding senior finance positions at Microsoft (MSFT), Cisco Systems (CSCO), and Texas Instruments (TXN). She helped oversee Nvidia's transformation into the dominant supplier of AI computing infrastructure, managing the financial complexities of its extraordinary expansion.
But perhaps her most important qualification for leading Nvidia is that she didn't act as a rubber stamp for Huang's ambitions.
Kress pushed back against some of Huang's aggressive multibillion-dollar AI investments, according to Reuters. While Huang wanted to accelerate Nvidia's influence across the industry, Kress was willing to question how much financial exposure the company should take on. That skepticism looks increasingly valuable.
Nvidia has moved well beyond selling chips. It has provided an estimated $300 billion in financial support to AI companies and cloud providers, some of which are also major customers. The arrangement helps finance the infrastructure boom that drives demand for Nvidia's products, but it also creates risks if customers struggle financially or AI spending slows.
Nvidia recorded $7.8 billion in gains on its equity investments during its fiscal second quarter. Those investments can strengthen the company's finances when valuations rise, but the reverse is equally true. Kress understands both sides of that equation, and was the one executive willing to push back on Huang's desire to aggressively finance the boom.
The chipmaker was also initially financially committed to OpenAI's Ohio data center project to the tune of $250 billion; Kress reportedly got it lowered to $120 billion.
Huang's greatest strength was recognizing where computing was headed before almost anyone else. His willingness to take enormous risks helped make Nvidia the centerpiece of the AI economy. But the company he leaves behind faces a different challenge.
Nvidia is no longer an underdog trying to establish a new market. It dominates an industry attracting hundreds of billions of dollars in investment. Maintaining that position requires more than technological leadership. It also demands careful capital allocation, disciplined risk management, and the confidence of shareholders increasingly concerned about the sustainability of AI spending.
Nvidia's financing ambitions illustrate the stakes. The company has partnered with major financial institutions to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure.
While that isn't $500 billion of Nvidia's own money, it demonstrates how deeply the chipmaker has become involved in financing the ecosystem that purchases its products. Kress may be better positioned to determine where supporting customers ends and assuming unnecessary financial risk begins.
Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Nov. 17, will give investors their first major opportunity to assess the company without Huang at the helm.
The business itself remains formidable. Nvidia reported $96.2 billion in second-quarter revenue, more than double the year-earlier figure, with its data center business generating $89 billion. Management subsequently projected third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.
Those numbers suggest Nvidia's immediate challenge isn't finding customers; it's ensuring that the tech giant's extraordinary revenue growth translates into durable profits without exposing shareholders to excessive financial risks.
Kress isn't guaranteed to be named Nvidia's permanent CEO. The board is said to be considering internal and external candidates, and her financial expertise doesn't automatically replace Huang's technical vision or relationships. Yet Nvidia already has an experienced engineering organization and an established technology roadmap. What investors may need most is someone willing to protect the financial foundation supporting those innovations.
Huang made Nvidia the king of AI. Kress could be the executive who ensures it remains one. For shareholders wondering whether Nvidia can keep thriving without its legendary founder, that may be the most encouraging possibility of all.
On the date of publication, Rich Duprey did not directly have a position in any of the securities mentioned in this article. All information and data in this article is solely for informational purposes. This article was originally published on Barchart.com

articles.title_orig: Prime Minister Carney advances Canada’s strategic partnership with China across trade, commerce, and culture
articles.title_zh: Prime Minister Carney advances Canada’s strategic partnership with China across trade, commerce, and culture
articles.content_orig:
Over the past year and a half, Canada’s government has recalibrated our relationship with China – strategically, pragmatically, and decisively. Last January, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, and the President of the People’s Republic of China, Xi Jinping, launched a new Canada-China strategic partnership to stabilise trade, build out clean energy industries, and better connect our peoples. Under the partnership, Canada and China have strengthened economic and financial cooperation, expanded cultural exchanges, and reduced tariffs on Canadian exports of canola seed and meal, peas, crab, and lobster. To date, Canada has restored market access for more than 90% of trade previously subject to tariff action – nearly $7.5 billion worth of Canadian exports.
To build on that success, Prime Minister Carney today met with President Xi in Shenzhen, China. The leaders agreed on new measures that will further expand trade between their two countries.
Canada and China are announcing:
To create more opportunities for investment, education, and exchanges between our countries, Prime Minister Carney announced:
The expanded partnership between Canada and China is also at play in the private sector. During the visit, Prime Minister Carney and President Xi welcomed the following agreements and investments from businesses:
The leaders also discussed the positive outcomes of recent dialogues between Canada and China to increase border and customs cooperation against narcotics threats, and to enhance collaboration on oil and gas, renewable energy, and nuclear with key industry leaders from the energy sector.
As the world’s second-largest economy and a country of more than 1.4 billion people, China plays a central role in Canada’s engagement in the Indo-Pacific. Across Canada, hundreds of thousands of jobs are supported by trade with China – from farmers in the Prairies to manufacturers in Ontario and Québec and fish harvesters in Atlantic Canada and British Columbia. Our trade with China generates over $30 billion in revenues and adds $6.9 billion to Canada’s GDP. By expanding Canada’s access to one of the world’s largest markets, we are opening new avenues for commercial, scientific, and cultural collaboration, and strengthening the ties between our peoples.
In Shenzhen, Prime Minister Carney will represent Canada at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ Meeting to further deepen our partnerships across the region.
“Canada and China have recalibrated our relationship to the benefit of citizens in both countries. We have unlocked billions in new export orders for Canadian farmers, ranchers, and fish harvesters – for workers and businesses across the country. We’re making it easier to travel, study, and do business between our nations to create more opportunity and prosperity for all. Canada is building our strength at home and diversifying our relationships abroad so that we have the freedom to live our lives as we choose.”
The Rt. Hon. Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada

articles.title_orig: Bessent pushed new AI chips rule
articles.title_zh: Bessent pushed new AI chips rule
articles.content_orig:
Ever since Donald Trump returned to the White House, flanked by a phalanx of supplicating tech billionaires, his administration has emphasized the need to win the A.I. race with China. Trump and his cronies have claimed repeatedly that we can’t constrain A.I. development because America needs to maintain an advantage over its chief geopolitical rival.
Yet the Nvidia scandal has revealed that the administration at best turned a blind eye when a leading American company gave an enormous boost to China’s A.I. industry, all while Trump and his cronies were profiting from it. Though the scandal started with sex — more precisely, the revelation that Jensen Huang, head of the company at the center of the A.I. boom, had an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy — it is really about the administration’s utterly careless attitude toward American security. And it demonstrates the bad faith behind its efforts to shove A.I. down our collective throats.
To understand why Trump’s tech policy has been such a national betrayal, it’s worth going back to Joe Biden’s administration. Ben Buchanan, who served as Biden’s White House special adviser for A.I., told me that America’s A.I. policy under Biden had two, interconnected pillars: slowing China down, and making sure that American A.I. was developed responsibly.
“It was our conviction that it would not be possible, or it would be much harder, to domestically regulate our companies if we were neck and neck with China,” said Buchanan, the author, along with his former colleague Tantum Collins, of an extremely well-timed new book about the global battle for A.I. supremacy, “The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World.” By denying China the chips that underpin advanced A.I. — most of which are made by Nvidia, and which China cannot yet replicate — the United States would try to maintain some control over the pace of A.I. growth.
When Donald Trump took over, he set about dismantling efforts to rein in A.I. On the first day of his second term, he revoked Biden’s executive order requiring the developers of frontier models to share the results of safety testing with the government. His administration has tried to block state-level A.I. regulation and limit the liability of A.I. developers should their systems harm people. When the N.A.A.C.P. filed a lawsuit accusing Elon Musk’s xAI of polluting Black neighborhoods in Mississippi with the makeshift power plants fueling two of his data centers, the Department of Justice intervened on Musk’s behalf.
Often, the rationale for these policies was the A.I. arms race with China. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in September. In response to mounting panic about A.I. escaping human control, Trump called the worriers “negative forces” and insisted that America had to retain its competitive edge. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he said.

US president Donald Trump heads to Asia this week to take part in back-to-back summits on economic cooperation, world conflicts, and nuclear weapons.
Much of the world’s focus will be on the historic, first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday.
However, hours before leaving the White House for the Philippines, Trump managed to raise the stakes even further while suggesting North Korean leader could also join them.
“(Xi) was here a month ago, and we're also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.
“So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.,” while stressing the decision on Kim’s attendance was up to Beijing.
Despite the strategic importance of the issues on the agenda during the trip, it could still be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal.
CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week after it emerged he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The ousted tech boss has close ties to the US president, even accompanying him on Air Force One during his last trip to China in May.
However Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
The US president is due tol land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, before flying to Shenzhen in southern China late on Wednesday for the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, at the end of which the first-ever three-way discussion between Xi, Trump, and ‌Putin will take place.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” said a White House spokesperson.
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February. It is the first time since the early 1970s that there is no legally binding limits on US and Russian nuclear forces without another agreement being under negotiation.
Russia and the US possess the largest nuclear arsenal in the world, followed by China.
The United Nations has long urged for nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tensions have fuelled nuclear risks around the world.
“If there is a denuclearisation program, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success,” UN ​Secretary-General Antonio ‌Guterres said on Monday in Manila, where he is attending the Asean summit.
The denuclearisation talks will also spotlight the war in Iran, with Tehran being a strategic partner of both China and Russia.
Leaders at Asean are likely to renew calls for peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including in the South China Sea and in Myanmar. They are expected to push for efforts to protect their economies and citizens from the continuing fallout from global conflicts, such as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
The White House has said that Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, while US officials will also meet on the sidelines with the so-called Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, which consists of Australia, India, Japan and the US.
Trump will be looking for an overseas success on the trip, following the disastrous midterm results that saw his Republican party lose control of Congress.
“The president will undoubtedly be seeking to use this trip to reassert leadership, authority, demonstrate his statesmanship capabilities and essentially show off on the international stage,” Kurt Tong, a former US ambassador for Apec, told Bloomberg.
The US president will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday.
But expectations for progress at the talks in China are not high. No agreement is expected afterward, a senior US official said, according to AP and Reuters.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” US-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling told PBS News .
“With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises,” he said.
Other critical issues at these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition.

articles.title_orig: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko at the site of a missile strike in October
Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October .
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day , the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.
Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
articles.title_zh: Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
articles.content_orig:
Japan scrambled fighter jets in its airspace after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its territory on Tuesday morning, an incident that could further strain ties between the two countries.
Tokyo said it had lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after the incident.
The aircraft entered Japan's airspace near Okinoshima in southwestern Japan shortly after 4:00 a.m. local time Tuesday (1900 GMT Monday), Japanese ​Chief Cabinet ‌Secretary Minoru Kihara ‌said.
"The violation of our national airspace by Russian aircraft is not only a grave infringement of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our security and is completely unacceptable," Kihara said.
"We lodged a very stern protest with Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly demanded measures to prevent any recurrence," he said.
Japan had lodged a similar protest with Russia in 2024 after a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times, marking the first confirmed incursion since 2019.
Kihara said the aircraft travelled through the Tsushima Strait and went between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before heading to the Pacific.
Japan's relations with Moscow have soured over the past weeks after a Japanese journalist was arrested on spying allegations and after Russia seized four of Japan Tobacco's Russian assets.
Russia and Japan share a decades-old dispute over the status of a number of islands in the Pacific Ocean .
However, relations especially deteriorated further after Tokyo joined global sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Tuesday's reported violation comes soon after South Korea said it too had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical maneuvers after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defense zone in the early hours of Tuesday.
An air defense zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.
Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defense zone, though this is not legally required.

articles.title_orig: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.title_zh: Major banking outage linked to Chase, impacted Wells Fargo and BofA
articles.content_orig:
Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and U.S. Bank are reportedly among the major banks experiencing widespread online outages.
JPMorgan Chase’s systems were coming back online Monday after an hourslong nationwide outage left customers reporting trouble withdrawing funds and accessing their bank accounts.
The disruption was traced to a software release the bank rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems, according to an FBI official. There was no indication of malicious or external cyber activity, the official said.
The impact was limited to JPMorgan Chase and transactions at other financial institutions in which JPMorgan Chase was a party, the official said.
The bank also said publicly that the incident was not malicious, and its systems were coming back online.
BANK OF AMERICA TO HIRE 1,000 MORE APPRENTICES, INVEST $150M IN WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT
After logging into the Chase app on November 16, during an online banking outage, one user reported seeing this error message. | Fox News
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," Chase said. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. This is a technical issue, not cyber-related."
Customers began reporting problems conducting transactions Monday morning. Chase earlier acknowledged an online banking issue in a response to a customer through its Chase Support account on X.
"We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking," Chase Support said. "Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience."
A teller at a Washington, D.C., Chase branch told FOX Business that in-store and online banking issues began around 10 a.m., and had been resolved just after 3 p.m. A branch manager said they had some glitches at the branch but can process most transactions there, on app and online. ATM machines were working as normal, the manager said.
At another branch, a Chase bank employee said the ATMs and banking app were working, but the computer system at the branch had "been up and down."
A JPMorgan Chase bank branch as customers experience disruptions due to a banking technology outage. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a company spokesperson said. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us."
Bank of America said its systems were operating normally.
"Bank of America systems have been operating normally today. Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information," the bank said in a statement.
LendingTree analyst Matt Schulz warns customers to watch for scammers exploiting confusion around reported Chase outages. His advice: verify updates directly with your bank and never share personal information with unsolicited callers or messages.
A spokesperson for US Bank also said its users were not experiencing issues.
"U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted," the spokesperson told Fox News. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delay."
BANK OF AMERICA UNVEILS $250B INITIATIVE TO MODERNIZE US INFRASTRUCTURE
PNC Financial Service and Wells Fargo told FOX Business they were not impacted by Monday's events.
Zelle, the digital payment network, said its system was working and operating as normal.
"Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," the company said in a statement. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
A JPMorgan Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
Zelle’s network operator is a company called Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo, according to The Associated Press.
The outage happened just a week after an historic FAA ground stop of air travel nationwide Friday and a Microsoft Outlook email disruption Thursday.

Last week’s widespread Microsoft 365 outage was driven by three factors, including a software bug undetected since July, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said Monday.
The trend continued Monday evening, with United Airlines reporting a system-wide computer outage.
"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience," the airlines told one person on X. "We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible. We appreciate your patience while we work through this."
United said the issue was resolved later Monday evening.
FOX Business' Ava Palschakov contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
The air traffic control tower at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in Los Angeles, California, on Nov. 14, 2026.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday blamed the previous day’s nationwide ground stop on the replacement of copper wires at a “remote” Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility. Installing new fiber optic lines led to critical communication breakdowns, he said.
About 7,500 flights were delayed and over 9,000 were canceled on Friday, according to FlightAware . Some 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. Eastern, shortly after the ground stop began.
The incident raised questions about what might have led to the historic event—only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11—and what authorities were doing to prevent it from happening again.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said Saturday, which saw nearly 6,000 additional flights canceled. "Or did they install a faulty router?"
As investigators continued working to pinpoint the source of the problem, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters in Washington, D.C., that disrupted flight schedules were expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday and promised that the “worst is behind us.”
While that may be true for this specific outage, Duffy warned Friday that what happened was not an isolated incident and said that outages would likely continue to occur until antiquated communications equipment across the FAA’s air traffic control network was brought up to date.
“It was the old legacy equipment. It failed,” Duffy said. “And listen, it’s going to continue to fail.”
The Transportation Secretary went on to call for Congress to provide $50 billion before the end of the year to upgrade air traffic control and airport infrastructure, increasing the administration’s recent $30.1 billion request, which included $10.1 billion specifically for air traffic control modernization.
President Donald Trump addressed the outage for the first time on Sunday, urging Congress to approve additional funding in a post on Truth Social . “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently,” he said.
There is reason to believe, however, that financial support alone will not solve the problems currently faced by the FAA. Those include shortages in fully certified air traffic controllers, weaknesses in planning and coordinating necessary modernization work, and vulnerabilities to cybersecurity threats.
TIME has reached out to Duffy’s office for comment.
Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic control system has been a goal of the industry for years, says Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, and billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“There has been a very methodical four-part, four-stage plan to upgrade that,” Booth tells TIME, referencing NextGen , a multibillion-dollar FAA modernization initiative dating to 2003. It has included shifting toward satellite-based aircraft tracking, digital communications, and more efficient flight routes.
Booth says a major focus of those earlier modernization efforts was making more efficient use of airspace.
“They have tried to squeeze more airplanes into limited space, make better use of the limited runways available in the system, and they started with completely changing the way airplanes are tracked in the world. It's a world standard now,” he says, pointing to how NextGen has already made strides in air travel.
The agency’s newer overhaul builds on earlier modernization work and includes replacing aging communications equipment, radar, and other infrastructure, with its first phase targeted for completion by the end of 2028.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
For more than two decades, the FAA has been working to modernize the NAS while fighting an uphill battle against aging infrastructure. The average U.S. air traffic control tower was 40 years old, and most radar systems were approaching that age, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves wrote in a May 2025 op-ed .
Congress had already ordered an independent review of the FAA’s aging technology: The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required an audit of legacy systems deployed before 2000—including their vulnerability to single-point failures—and a plan to accelerate replacement or improvement of those found to pose risks. In a written response to Congress , the FAA said that nonprofit research organization MITRE completed the audit in August 2025. The response said the findings would guide modernization efforts, but did not disclose the specific findings or resulting actions.
In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA to upgrade its “radar, software, hardware, and telecommunications” at more than 4,600 sites through December 2028.
As of Nov. 5, the FAA said it has “replaced 69% of copper wires, installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers, transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips [and] installed 226 IP Voice Switches.”
The updates were noted within an announcement saying the FAA was beginning to phase out the floppy disks used in air traffic control. It said that it had launched a replacement system that would include a digital display board with data about disruptions, weather conditions, and advisories. The announcement identified five initial facilities and set a goal of installing the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.
Duffy called these efforts “the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
The FAA then announced Nov. 10 that it was expanding its AI-powered scheduling and flight-planning tool—known as SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories)—to airspace managed by all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide. SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million contract that also covers the agency’s Flow Management Data and Services program.
Duffy said at Friday’s press conference that SMART had nothing to do with the disruption.
Describing Friday's outage, Duffy said a router being replaced as workers switched from copper wiring to fiber-optic connections began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting communications and some radar feeds. Systems came back online after officials isolated the work at the remote location, he said.
For Booth, the spread of that disruption underscores the need for safeguards that can contain a problem in one part of the FAA’s communications network before it affects the wider system.
“They need a system that is not prone to single-point failures,” he says.
Booth pointed out that legacy systems—often relying on analog lines, decades-old routers, and interconnected regional hubs—lack the fault-tolerant design needed to prevent a local or routine maintenance glitch from cascading nationwide.
“The public probably would be shocked to learn that the way pilots communicate with air traffic control is tantamount to an old-fashioned telephone line,” he says. “You've got 10, sometimes 15 airplanes competing to talk to a single controller-specified frequency.”
Kumar Sokka, the CEO of Acre Security, says a key consideration when upgrading complex systems is whether individual components can fail without disrupting the entire network.
“Can you remove a single point of failure? Are these systems distributed in a way where it's siloed in certain structures where if something fails, not everything fails, right?” asks Sokka.
He says that many industries come up against issues of balancing the high upfront expense of upgrading legacy systems against the severe financial and operational risks of future outages.

articles.title_orig: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.title_zh: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.content_orig:
An aerial shows a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction on Oct. 29, 2026 in Vernon, California.
America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability .
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models , has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers .
American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
“Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.
The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.
They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.
More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark.
Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.
However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
“For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.”
Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF.
The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.
The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.
“We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

articles.title_orig: Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s Daughter, Became a Powerful Force at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Madison Huang, Jensen Huang’s Daughter, Became a Powerful Force at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Who are the family members of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang?
Over the years, Huang has told anecdotes about buying his parents a Mercedes, and about meeting his wife and her importance to his early days. His two kids, Spencer and Madison, worked for him at Nvidia. His mother and father emigrated from Taiwan, and Huang's childhood helped forge his success in the U.S. It was a towering success story, that is, until he resigned on November 12 amid an inquiry into alleged affairs, including one with a possible Chinese spy.
Here's what you need to know about Huang's parents, wife, and children.
Huang, who is one of the richest men in the world with a net worth of around $147 billion, sold shares "to buy his parents a luxury Mercedes S-Class."
He joked it was the most expensive car in the world," Yahoo Finance reported.
"My only regret was after the IPO—I wanted to buy my parents something nice, so I sold Nvidia stock at a valuation of $300 million," Huang said, adding, "They regret it."  He added that his parents still have the vehicle.
According to Reuters , Jensen Huang "emigrated to the United States as a child." He started Nvidia, a leader in artificial intelligence, in 1993.
The family's immigration story is told by Britannica Money. "Huang was born the second son of Taiwan citizens Huang Hsing-tai and Lo Tsai-hsiu. Huang's father was a chemical engineer, and his mother taught grade school," that site says. "When he was five, the family moved to Thailand . However, due to the then-ongoing Vietnam War , Huang's parents decided that they wouldn't settle in Thailand permanently."
Huang's father went to work for an "American air conditioner manufacturer" and "had formed a positive impression of the United States." According to Britannic, Huang's mother helped "prepare Huang and his brother for the eventual move by teaching them 10 random English words a day."
Huang went to live with an uncle in Tacoma, Washington, at age 9 until his parents could come to the U.S, and he attended the "all-boys Oneida Baptist Institute in rural Oneida, Kentucky, mistakenly believing it to be a prestigious boarding school." In fact, it was a "religious reform school," Britannica reported, and Huang and his brother faced mistreatment there. He eventually rejoined his parents in Portland.
According to his biography on the website of the Oregon State engineering program Huang was "a young immigrant to the United States from his native Taiwan," when "he was inadvertently placed with his older brother in a reform school in rural Kentucky and received what he has described as a 'hard knocks' introduction to this country."
Huang met wife Lori when he was 17 and they were lab partners in a college engineering class, the Oregon State bio says, adding that they married five years later.
According to Britannica, she is the former Lori Mills.
She is also an electrical engineer who helps run the family's foundation, and she is the mother of his son Spencer and daughter Madison, who both work for Nvidia (and who have been floated as potential successors. According to Yahoo Finance , "Nvidia said in its fiscal 2026 proxy filing that Madison Huang and Spencer Huang, children of CEO Jensen Huang, received total compensation of approximately $1.23 million and $1.32 million , respectively, for the year ended January 25, 2026."

articles.title_orig: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.title_zh: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo's team-based squid-shooter Splatoon 3 is still going strong, and this week the title is getting updated to Version 12.0.0 .
This major update will come with changes to multiplayer, including weapon adjustments. There are also changes to Anarchy Battle, X Battles and challenges. Additionally, there are changes to the GameChat feature on Switch 2. Nintendo also notes how its next update after this one will focus on multiplayer game balance .
You can get the full rundown in the official patch notes below ( via Nintendo's official support page ):
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Sections marked "on Nintendo Switch 2" apply only to Nintendo Switch 2. All other changes apply to both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch.
Made it possible to participate with a friend in traditional X Battles as a group of two.
Added a feature that allows players to open GameChat and invite friends from their group while playing modes with friends, such as battles or Salmon Run.
This update focuses on making changes to matchmaking and multiplayer balance.
For X Battles, we have added a feature to allow players to play as a pair with a friend. The goal of this feature is to expand the range of ways to play, and we will introduce it on a trial basis starting in Chill Season 2026. After we have introduced it, we will comprehensively analyze how these battles are actually played and how the gameplay situation shifts, including for players who are not playing with a friend. Then we will decide whether to continue providing this feature in future seasons.
For Anarchy Battle (Series), we have changed the matchmaking system such that, in exchange for removing the feature allowing players to continue with the same team, matchmaking will now complete more quickly and with less imbalance of skill level and equipped weapons between players and their opponents.
For Challenges, we have changed how Challenge Power is calculated to make it easier to raise Challenge Power the more wins a player has. With this change, between players who would have ended up with about the same Challenge Power under the previous system, the player who attained the greater number of wins will have the higher final Challenge Power.
For multiplayer balance, we made a variety of changes to main, sub, and special weapons, including changes to the flight distance of Blaster shots.
With most weapons, when a player fires while moving, the player's movement speed is added to the shot's speed to a certain extent, resulting in a more natural trajectory. For Blasters, we have minimized the change in shot flight distance caused by this effect, making it easier to maintain an appropriate distance against an opponent’s Blaster.
Among the special weapons, we have changed the Reefslider because, while there is statistically little impact on victories in matches between extremely skilled players, it has a high impact on matches between less skilled players. The intention behind this change is to alleviate that striking difference. By narrowing the area affected by the explosion we have made it so that players cannot reap the maximum benefit without using it at the precise position. On the other hand, we have extended the invulnerability period to make it harder for opponents who used terrain to survive the explosion to counterattack and easier for the player to make follow-up attacks.
For the Tenta Missiles, we have decreased the vulnerability while firing and expanded the area where it is possible to lock on to opponents. As a result, it will now be easier to use, even in situations where opponents are nearby the player. By decreasing the impact interval, it becomes easier to defeat opponents who are slow to dodge, but the duration for which they must keep dodging is reduced.
We have also added a feature for Nintendo Switch 2 that will make it easier to use GameChat.
The next update will focus on changes to multiplayer balance.
If you haven't already played the game on Switch 2, there's a free upgrade available which includes visual improvements and frame rate optimisations for the platform. In some related news, Splatoon Raiders has also received an eShop demo this week!

articles.title_orig: Jared Kushner’s $500M Trump Hotel Dream in Serbia Officially Crumbles
articles.title_zh: Jared Kushner’s $500M Trump Hotel Dream in Serbia Officially Crumbles
articles.content_orig:
Serbia's government has terminated its agreement with a company linked to Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, to redevelop Belgrade's former General Staff military headquarters, the construction ministry confirmed to Serbian media on November 14.
The Ministry of Construction, Transport and Infrastructure told public broadcaster RTS and weekly Vreme that a termination agreement was being finalised and was expected to be completed early next week, bringing an end to a controversial project that sparked protests and a criminal investigation.
A government source told Vreme that the agreement with Kushner's Atlantic Incubation Partners LLC had been terminated, with both parties waiving all mutual claims. This would rule out arbitration proceedings or financial penalties against Serbia over the cancellation, the source said.
The formal termination follows the company's withdrawal from the project in December 2025 and comes during a political transition after the October 25 parliamentary election, in which a student-led electoral list defeated the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), ending its more than decade-long hold on power.
Approved by the government in May 2024, the project envisaged a luxury hotel, residential and commercial buildings, and a museum on the site of the former Yugoslav military headquarters, which was heavily damaged during NATO's 1999 bombing campaign against Yugoslavia.
The removal of the complex's protected cultural heritage status was a precondition for the development. The government's decision to revoke the protection in November 2024 triggered protests by architects, heritage experts, students and other citizens, who argued that the buildings were an important example of Serbian modernist architecture and a memorial to NATO's bombing campaign.
The controversy also led to an investigation by Serbia's organised crime prosecution office into alleged falsification of documents and abuse of office in the process of removing the site's protected status. In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials.
Selaković has denied wrongdoing and described the proceedings as politically motivated. The trial is scheduled to resume on November 23, after a hearing earlier this month was postponed because one of the defendants was hospitalised.
Former president Aleksandar Vučić had strongly backed the development, saying it would bring €750mn in investment and create between 1,500 and 3,000 construction jobs.

articles.title_orig: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
articles.title_zh: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
articles.content_orig:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan’s top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, in an open letter released by his lawyer.
Lawyer Salman Safdar posted the letter on X on Monday, describing it as a “humanitarian plea for medical treatment”. It is Khan’s first such letter since he fell ill earlier this year.
Safdar said Khan gave him instructions and notes during a three-hour meeting at Central Jail Rawalpindi, also known as Adiala Jail, on November 11, and that he prepared the letter solely on that basis.
Khan, 74, has been in jail since August 2023, following convictions that his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), says are politically motivated.
In the letter, he said he had been held in solitary confinement “for up to twenty-two hours a day” since December 20, 2025, when he and Bushra Bibi were sentenced to 17 years in one of several cases against them.
He said he had lost 85 percent of the vision in his right eye and that doctors had told him he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.
Khan wrote that he had “never once sought relief on medical grounds, nor used illness as a tactic”.
“I fought on the merits, with confidence, and I still do,” he said. “I do not ask Your Lordships for any favour.”
On August 18, the Supreme Court ordered that Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days and examined by a medical board. “That order has not been implemented,” he wrote.
Instead, he was taken to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) and returned to jail within hours.
Khan was taken to hospital again late on November 10 for an eye injection. PIMS said he was “clinically stable”, while Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said he was receiving the required care.
Khan also raised concerns about Bushra Bibi, whom he married in 2018. He said she suffered a retinal detachment in April and underwent “complicated eye surgery in secrecy”.
Without another operation, he said, “she may lose her sight permanently”.
Her lawyers filed an application at the Islamabad High Court on Monday seeking her complete medical record and immediate transfer to a specialised hospital.
Two of Khan’s sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were released from a Lahore jail on November 12 after nearly two months in detention. Aleema Khan, a third sister, remains in jail, according to PTI.
The government said it detained the sisters over a possible threat to law and order in advance of PTI’s Islamabad march planned for September 27, which did not go ahead.
Sayed Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader, said ex-PM Khan had been left with no other option but to seek further legal intervention.
“He’s been left with no choice but to write this open letter because, over three years of imprisonment and solitary confinement, he has seen that justice has only been seen in small flashes and then gone away,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera.
Bukhari said the letter did not mean Khan was giving up.
“He is asking for no favours. He is asking for no deal. He is asking for justice and the legal system of Pakistan to work,” Bukhari told Al Jazeera. “All it shows is a man humbly asking for justice and humane medical treatment.”
Bukhari said the party wanted the courts to press the government to act.
“We want the courts to hear his proceedings adequately … rather than adjourning and postponing them,” he said. “And we want the courts to apply enough pressure on the government that real medical treatment should be provided so that there is no loss of life, no loss of vision.”
Mehmal Sarfraz, a Lahore-based political analyst, said the letter reflected Khan’s concern about his wife’s health.
“He is very worried about his wife’s deteriorating health and is looking for relief for her,” Sarfraz told Al Jazeera.
Another Lahore-based political analyst, Habib Akram, said he did not see the letter as a plea for mercy.
“If he were asking for mercy, he would not have needed to write this letter. He has written to the courts, not to anyone else,” Akram told Al Jazeera. “And what is he asking for? He is asking for his rights, which he has cited from the jail manual.”
Akram, however, was sceptical that the letter would change Khan’s circumstances.
“What is being done to Imran Khan has lost its legal grounds. The Islamabad High Court has an order that he can meet visitors on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The Supreme Court has also ruled. Neither was followed, but a third order was suddenly complied with,” he said.
“This is no longer a legal issue. I don’t think the Supreme Court’s order will be implemented because of this letter.”
